extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of comedy, playwrights, literary critics, and theorists of humour
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying theoretical principles that explain what makes situations, words, characters, and actions comic (with emphasis on stage/playwriting and general literary comedy). Useful for critics, dramatists, and students of humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Something mechanical encrusted upon the living
rubrics_metrics.description: The central law: comic effect arises from 'something mechanical encrusted upon the living' — an artificial/machine-like element superposed on life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the root image from which many comic forms derive; it covers mechanisation of body, of society, and the transformation of persons into things. Use examples of machines/pupets/automatons superposed on people or social life. The chapter repeatedly returns to this image as the starting point for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremony/form isolated from matter
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘For any ceremony, then, to become comic, it is enough that our attention be fixed on the ceremonial element in it, and that we neglect its matter.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attention is shifted from purpose/content to the form or ritual itself the ceremony loses seriousness and becomes laughable. Applicable to prize-distributions, court sittings, formal etiquette. To create comic effect, foreground the ritual/form and disregard the underlying purpose; anti-pattern: if the substance is emphasized, the comic is lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative automatism and pedantry
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete automatism — officials or regulations acting like machines and enforcing rules with inexorable fatality — produces comedy (pedantry as art pretending to outdo nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit the clash between human situations and rigid, rule-bound responses (customs officers asking rescued shipwreck victims if they have anything to declare; MPs applying company rules to murder). Use examples of professional ritualism (doctors, judges, lawyers) and aphoristic statements that treat regulation as law of nature. Anti-pattern: realistic, sympathetic portrayals of officials remove the mechanistic humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body intruding on the moral/intellectual (body vs. soul)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Any incident is comic that calls our attention to the physical in a person, when it is the moral side that is concerned.’ The intrusion of bodily/material concerns into moral/intellectual moments creates laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common devices: bodily mishaps during solemn speech (sneeze), symptoms of the body interrupting dignity (toothache, tight shoes), excess stoutness, bashfulness as bodily embarrassment. In drama, avoid bodily actions in tragedy to prevent unintended comic effects (e.g., don't have tragic heroes sit/eat/drink). To make comic, juxtapose high moral/intellectual tone with crude physical reminders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person giving the impression of being a thing
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘We laugh every time a person gives us the impression of being a thing.’ Comic images derive from treating persons as objects or events rather than agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques: portray people as bundles, balls, dummies, or events (e.g., listing people as parcels; calling kings 'that have occurred'). Circus/clown business that erases humanness (bodies becoming balls or wooden dummies) exemplifies this. Partial identification (confusing person with function) suffices to produce the effect. Anti-pattern: vivid individualization that preserves humanity reduces this comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: The illusion of life combined with the impression of mechanism (situational law)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Any arrangement of acts and events is comic which gives us, in a single combination, the illusion of life and the distinct impression of a mechanical arrangement.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For situations: construct scenes where characters behave with lifelike motive yet their sequence or structure exposes a mechanical pattern (Jack-in-the-box, Punch and Judy rhythms). Balance 'life' (motivation) and 'mechanism' (pattern) so the audience perceives both simultaneously. If scene feels wholly natural or wholly mechanical, the intended comic blend is weakened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and the 'spring' (jack-in-the-box) device
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition (the bent-and-released spring) — repeated words, actions, returns — is a fundamental comic process: the recurrence marks tempo and produces laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhythmic recurrence of phrases, entrances/exits, or actions to create comic momentum (Punch & Judy, recurring curses/exclamations, characters reappearing like a jack-in-the-box). The tempo and predictable return are essential; vary degree and timing for crescendo. Anti-pattern: repetition without variation or purpose becomes tedious rather than comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication of ridiculousness across layers (overtones)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic 'overtones': when a primary ridiculous notion (appearance triumphing over reality) automatically evokes subsidiary ridiculous images — e.g., professional ridiculousness is reinforced by physical defect (speech defect echoing intellectual ossification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting comic characters, pair a professional/formal absurdity with a matching physical trait or mannerism to create sympathetic 'overtones' (a stammering judge signaling intellectual rigidity). This instinctive duplication strengthens the comic impression. Anti-pattern: mismatched or absent physical cues can blunt the intended connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of suggestion and acceptability of the joke
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke's effectiveness depends on giving it 'power of suggestion' so it seems the natural product of a mind-state or consistent with the circumstances; otherwise it won't be accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure jokes arise plausibly from character and situation (e.g., a father's repeated use of a phrase in lessons explains a child's odd phrasing). The comic must feel organic (natural product) or contextually appropriate; forced or contextless jokes risk failing. Consider frequency, precedent, and plausibility when inserting a gag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual suggestion: moving from vague to distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of inducing comic images by gradually making perceptions more indefinite and then concretizing them — the slow solidification from dim, fluid impressions into a precise comic image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include graduated hints (like hypnotic suggestion), rhythmic/poetic devices (rhythm, rhyme, assonance) that lull the imagination and then crystallize an image (e.g., Régnard lines or Figaro's rapid descriptors). Use gradual escalation or accumulated hints to make an improbable image acceptable. Anti-pattern: abrupt, unsupported images that the audience cannot be led to accept.
